title: How Weather Modification Works
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with rainy-weather banter (Atlanta rain, 2007 Georgia governor Sonny Perdue's prayer for rain, Romanian Papa Ruta rain dance) and then examine weather modification. They cover early cloud seeding experiments by Henry Houghton (MIT) and Vincent Schaefer-era figures such as Harvard's Emory Leon Chaffee, Bernard Vonnegut's silver iodide discovery and the warm-cloud salt method, GE's Project Cirrus hurricane seeding in 1947, Irving Langmuir's claims, the 1948 New Mexico and Kansas flood controversy, the 1952 British Royal Air Force seeding in Devon and the Lynmouth flood, Operation Popeye in Vietnam, US-Soviet talks and the ENMOD treaty banning hostile weather modification, China's Beijing Olympics cloud-shooting, the National Hail Research Experiment in Colorado's Hail Alley, hurricane-thwarting ideas, airport fog dissipation and de-icing, and whether cloud seeding actually works. Ends with shout-outs (Kiva team, photographer Bill Wadman) and listener mail about a Scottish homeless man repaying a gift.

segments.title: Rainy day banter and rain rituals
segments.summary: Hosts talk about rain in Atlanta and a drought, Governor Sonny Perdue's 2007 prayer for rain, the Pueblo rain dance, and the Romanian Papa Ruta rain ritual.

segments.title: Early attempts at rainmaking and Vonnegut's silver iodide
segments.summary: Early twentieth-century scientists tried to make rain or stop fog, including Henry Houghton at MIT and Emory Leon Chaffee at Harvard. Bernard Vonnegut found silver iodide's crystal structure resembles ice and used it to seed supercooled clouds, creating convective updrafts.

segments.title: Warm clouds and salt seeding
segments.summary: For warm clouds above zero degrees Celsius, the method is to dump table salt or sand, which attracts water to form raindrops, requiring large amounts delivered by plane or ground station.

segments.title: GE Project Cirrus and the 1947 hurricane
segments.summary: General Electric ran dry ice seeding experiments, with snowfall in Schenectady. Partnering with the Army as Project Cirrus, they dumped dry ice into an Atlantic hurricane in October 1947, which then changed course toward Georgia and killed several people. Irving Langmuir believed they had caused it, while another scientist argued a similar 1906 hurricane followed the same path.

segments.title: Kansas rain claims, British and Vietnam operations
segments.summary: Claims of cloud seeding in New Mexico causing rain in Kansas and floods were debated; Langmuir and Vonnegut urged restraint. The Royal Air Force seeded clouds over southwest England, followed by heavy rain and the Lynmouth flood that killed 35 people. In 1967 the US tried to extend monsoon season on the Ho Chi Minh trail in Operation Popeye.

segments.title: Weather warfare treaty and China's cloud-shooting
segments.summary: After a reporter exposed Operation Popeye, the US and Soviets held talks on banning weather modification, which stalled over tactical versus strategic uses. The UN produced the ENMOD Convention banning hostile geophysical weather modification. China's weather modification program shot silver iodide rockets at clouds before the Beijing Olympics.

segments.title: Hail suppression, hurricanes, fog, and effectiveness
segments.summary: The National Hail Research Experiment in Hail Alley was cut short; farmers opposed seeding and a radar truck was dynamited in the San Luis Valley. Ideas for thwarting hurricanes are discussed, including Bill Gates' patent. Airports use seeding, heating and propane to dissipate fog and de-ice planes. The hosts conclude that effectiveness is unproven, with the American Meteorological Society estimating about a ten percent increase in precipitation.
